summary_rationale: CVE exposure, high static/shared third-party library usage, and legacy dependency evidence support vulnerability/configuration exploitation as a strongly supported software-side attack category.
Shell-injection and third-party tool invocation evidence directly support build/toolchain compromise as a strongly supported software supply-chain category.

Maintainer-count evidence indirectly supports trusted identity or maintainer compromise because larger maintainer/dependency exposure can increase the number of trusted identities in the software supply-chain surface.

The current evidence pass uses tool behavior, dependency exposure, CVEs, TPL percentages, and Figure 3 library exposure; it does not directly measure package introduction, package confusion, typosquatting, or package misselection.
The current evidence pass does not directly include repository compromise, source-code tampering, or malicious commits.
The current evidence pass does not directly measure package hosting, mirrors, downloads, or update-channel compromise.
The current evidence pass does not directly measure signature verification, signing keys, release integrity checks, or verification bypasses.
TPL percentage, Figure 3 library exposure, and artifact/config access evidence strongly support the capability where consumed software components can influence tool behavior.
High-risk CVE evidence from Yosys, OpenSTA, and OpenLane directly supports vulnerability/configuration-based software control as a strongly supported capability.
Shell-injection and third-party tool invocation evidence directly support toolchain execution control across HLS, verification, placement/routing, and signoff-related tools.
Maintainer-count evidence indirectly supports trusted project or maintainer access because larger dependency-maintainer exposure increases the trusted identity surface.
The current evidence pass does not directly measure source repository modification, malicious commits, or repository write access.
The current evidence pass does not directly measure developer machines, maintainer environments, credentials, or local build environments.
The current evidence pass does not directly measure update channels, mirrors, package hosting, binary distribution, or download compromise.
The current evidence pass does not directly measure signing keys, signature checks, verification bypasses, or release authentication.
Static dependency exposure and artifact/config access in synthesis tools indirectly support design tampering because compromised tool behavior may modify or reinterpret design inputs.

Artifact/configuration access in synthesis, DFT, and manufacturing-test tools indirectly supports access abuse or disruption because software-side manipulation can reach important design/test artifacts.
High static dependency exposure in Yosys indirectly supports Trojan/backdoor plausibility, but this evidence alone does not directly show Trojan insertion or trigger behavior.
No direct evidence row in this v1 mapping is attached to information leakage yet; this category should be supported later through case-study evidence or file-access/leakage-specific evidence.
The current evidence pass does not directly include IP theft, unauthorized copying, counterfeit use, or design-asset exfiltration evidence.
The current evidence pass does not directly measure side-channel leakage, fault injection, physical attack behavior, or physical-trigger conditions.
Although HLS tools appear in the raw evidence, this v1 mapping does not directly show HLS-specific security vulnerability insertion or HLS semantic transformation errors.
The current evidence pass does not directly measure IC replacement, chip substitution, or physical/manufacturing substitution evidence.
